promptText: How should a startup founder working solo organize their team's work?
rawText:
When you are a solo founder, the phrase "team’s work" effectively means **organizing your own time across multiple roles**, while setting up systems to manage external help (contractors, freelancers, AI, and future hires). 

To avoid burnout and context-switching fatigue, you need to treat your solo startup like a structured organization. Here is a step-by-step framework to organize your work effectively.

---

### 1. "Departmentalize" Yourself
As a solo founder, you are simultaneously the CEO, Product Manager, Lead Developer/Creator, Marketer, and Customer Support agent. If you switch between these roles randomly throughout the day, your productivity will plummet.

*   **Time-Theme Your Days (Maker vs. Manager):**
    *   **Monday & Friday (Manager Days):** High-level strategy, finance, content planning, outreach, and administrative tasks.
    *   **Tuesday–Thursday (Maker Days):** Deep work. Coding, product design, core content creation, or heavy building. Block off calls entirely on these days.
*   **Wear One Hat at a Time:** Decide which "role" you are playing during any given time block. If you are in "Developer Mode," ignore marketing notifications.

---

### 2. Set Up a "Single Source of Truth"
Do not keep your roadmap in your head. Set up a simple project management hub using tools like **Notion, Trello, Linear, or Asana**.

Organize your workspace into four basic buckets:
1.  **Backlog (The Icebox):** Ideas, feature requests, and future marketing campaigns. (Get them out of your head so you don't feel overwhelmed).
2.  **Current Sprint (This Week):** 3 to 5 critical tasks that move the business forward *this week*.
3.  **In Progress:** What you are actively working on today (limit this to 1–2 tasks max).
4.  **Done:** Celebrating wins builds momentum.

> **Rule of Thumb:** If a tool takes more than 30 minutes a week to maintain, it is too complex for a solo founder. Keep it lean.

---

### 3. Build SOPs (Standard Operating Procedures) Early
Even if you are working alone today, document your processes as if you are hiring someone tomorrow.

*   **"Rule of Two":** If you have to perform a task more than twice (e.g., publishing a blog post, onboarding a beta user, releasing a software update), document the exact steps in a checklist.
*   **Use Screen Recordings:** Use **Loom** to record yourself doing repetitive tasks while talking through your thought process. 
*   **Why this helps:** When you eventually hire a freelancer or VA, you can hand over the Loom video and SOP instantly without spending hours training them.

---

### 4. Leverage the "Invisible Team" (AI & Automation)
Before hiring human team members, automate and delegate to software.

*   **Automation:** Use **Zapier** or **Make** to connect your tools. (e.g., Automatically send customer feedback from a web form straight to your task manager).
*   **AI Assistants:** Treat AI (ChatGPT, Claude, Cursor, GitHub Copilot) as junior employees:
    *   *Use AI for:* First drafts of copy, writing boilerplate code, brainstorming marketing angles, or summarizing customer feedback.
    *   *Your job:* Edit, review, and make high-level decisions.

---

### 5. Managing External Support (Contractors & Freelancers)
When you do hire freelancers (designers, copywriters, specialized devs), treat them like a synchronous team by relying on **Asynchronous Communication**:

*   **Over-Communicate Context:** Don't just give contractors a task; give them the *goal* behind the task.
*   **Use Loom over Meetings:** Instead of a 30-minute Zoom call to explain a visual change or bug, record a 3-minute Loom video.
*   **Centralized Deliverables:** Keep all deliverables, links, and feedback inside your project management tool (Notion/Asana) so client/contractor history isn't buried in Slack or email threads.

---

### 6. Establish a Solo Operating Cadence
Without a boss or co-founder, you need a rhythm to stay accountable.

*   **Daily (5 minutes):** Pick **1 Big Thing (The "Frog")** to accomplish today. Complete it before checking email or social media.
*   **Weekly (30 minutes on Friday):** Conduct a "Solo Retrospective":
    *   *What did I accomplish this week?*
    *   *What blocked me?*
    *   *What is the main priority for next week?*
*   **Quarterly:** Review your macro goals (revenue targets, product milestones) and adjust course.

---

### Summary Checklist for the Solo Founder:

| Category | Action Item | Tool Example |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Schedule** | Block deep-work days vs. admin days. | Google Calendar |
| **Tasks** | Maintain a lightweight Kanban board. | Notion, Linear, Trello |
| **Processes** | Record Loom videos of repetitive tasks. | Loom, Notion Docs |
| **Scale** | Automate workflows between apps. | Zapier, Make |
| **Execution** | Pick 1 "Must-Do" priority per day. | Pen & Paper |
